body.statement: Let \(K\geq3\), \(m\geq3\), \(1\leq i\leq m-1\), and \(2i\neq m\). For \(C=((m-i)e_0+ie_L,\ ie_0+(m-i)e_L)\) and \(C'=C^\top\), one has \(d(C,C')=3\).
body.justification: This theorem certifies that three heterogeneous units are genuinely necessary in the worst nonbinary balanced case, rather than an artifact of the cubic construction.
body.gap: Neither exact binary test inversion in \cite{RigdonHudgens2015} nor generic group testing in \cite{HemerikGoeman2018} studies the optimal sparse legal-schedule certificate number.
body.consumer: It fixes the smallest worst-case adversarial schedule size that a balanced nonbinary symmetry classifier must include in a software audit.
body.proof_tex:
Put \(j=m-i\). The profiles in the statement have endpoint coordinates
\[
 h_0=j,quad h_L=i,qquad g_0=i,quad g_L=j,
 \tag{1}
\]
and all interior coordinates vanish. The hypotheses \(1\leq i\leq m-1\) give \(i,j>0\), so the pair is not \(\{C_+,C_-\}\); the hypothesis \(2i\neq m\) gives \(i\neq j\), so the profiles are distinct transposes. Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}alphabet\text{-}frontier}\) therefore proves inequivalence and \(d(C,C')\leq3\). We prove the reverse inequality.

Fix \(R\in\mathcal R_0(n,K)\) with \(q(R)\leq2\). If \(q(R)=0\), every unit is diagonal. Proposition \(\mathrm{prop{:}diagonal\text{-}reduction}\) gives zero count for both profiles unless \(R=D_{me_0+me_L}\); for that table, Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}assignment\text{-}count}\) and binomial symmetry give
\[
 W_R(C)=\binom mj\binom mi
 =\binom mi\binom mj=W_R(C').
 \tag{2}
\]
The case \(q(R)=1\) is impossible: all diagonal units contribute zero to the weak-null sum, whereas the unique heterogeneous unit contributes a nonzero integer \(a-b\), contradicting Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}weak\text{-}null}\).

It remains to consider \(q(R)=2\). Label the two heterogeneous units by their response types \((a,b)\) and \((c,d)\), with repeated table cells represented by separate labeled units. Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}weak\text{-}null}\) says
\[
 a+c=b+d.
 \tag{3}
\]
If any diagonal filler unit has an interior outcome, it is observed at that interior level under every assignment, so both endpoint-only profiles have count zero. We may therefore assume all diagonal filler units lie at \(0\) or \(L\). Partition the labeled assignments according to the four treatment statuses of the two special units.

If both special units are treated and contribute nonzero count, then \(a,c\in\{0,L\}\). They cannot both be zero, since (3) and nonnegativity would imply \(b=d=0\); they cannot both be \(L\), since (3) and \(b,d\leq L\) would imply \(b=d=L\). Either conclusion would contradict heterogeneity. Hence their treated outcomes have multiset \(\{0,L\}\), and a nonzero count requires \(m-1\) diagonal filler units at each endpoint. The filler-selection coefficients for \(C\) and \(C'\) are, respectively,
\[
 \binom{m-1}{j-1}\binom{m-1}{i-1}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \binom{m-1}{i-1}\binom{m-1}{j-1},
 \tag{4}
\]
so they agree. If both special units are controlled, the same argument applied to \(b,d\) gives equal coefficients
\[
 \binom{m-1}{j}\binom{m-1}{i}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \binom{m-1}{i}\binom{m-1}{j}.
 \tag{5}
\]

Now suppose the first special unit is treated and the second is controlled. If either observed outcome \(a,d\) is interior, both contributions vanish. If \(a,d\in\{0,L\}\) are different, then (3) forces both response types to be diagonal. For example, \((a,d)=(0,L)\) gives \(c-b=L\), hence \((c,b)=(L,0)\); the reverse case is symmetric. This contradicts heterogeneity. Therefore a nonzero contribution requires \(a=d=v\) for some \(v\in\{0,L\}\). Equation (3) then gives \(b=c=u\), so the two response types are \((v,u)\) and \((u,v)\), with \(u\neq v\). One special observation of \(v\) lies in each arm. Consequently the diagonal filler contains \(m-2\) units at \(v\) and \(m\) at the opposite endpoint \(\bar v=L-v\). The two coefficients are
\[
 \binom{m-2}{h_v-1}\binom m{h_{\bar v}}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \binom{m-2}{g_v-1}\binom m{g_{\bar v}}.
 \tag{6}
\]
They agree because (1) implies \(h_v+g_v=m\) and \(h_{\bar v}+g_{\bar v}=m\), and hence each binomial coefficient is the complementary one. The other mixed treatment status is identical after exchanging the two labels.

The four cases exhaust every labeled assignment, so (4)--(6) and Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}assignment\text{-}count}\) imply \(W_R(C)=W_R(C')\) for every legal \(R\) with \(q(R)\leq2\). The positive common normalizer in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}randomization\text{-}kernel}\) gives equality of the corresponding probabilities. Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}separator\text{-}size}\) therefore yields \(d(C,C')\geq3\), which with the upper bound proves \(d(C,C')=3\).

For the requested finite early-kill audit, take \(K=3\), \(m=3\), \(L=2\), and \(i=1\). The cubic construction in (10) of the proof of Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}alphabet\text{-}frontier}\) is
\[
 R=E_{20}+2E_{01}+E_{00}+2E_{22}.
\]
Its mass is six and its weak-null effect sum is \(2-2=0\). Direct expansion over all \(\binom63=20\) balanced assignments gives count \(1\) for \(C=((2,0,1),(1,0,2))\) and count \(0\) for \(C'=C^{\mathsf T}\). Independently enumerating the nonnegative \(3\times3\) integer tables of mass six, imposing the weak-null equation and \(q(R)\leq2\), leaves \(103\) tables; the exhaustive four-status argument above gives equal counts for this pair for every one. This computation is a check of, and not a premise for, the all-size proof.
